Good afternoon, and welcome to the last panel of the day. The topic is technology and disruption in infrastructure, and we have a very simple format. I will ask each panelist one question, and I would like a one-minute answer. Not a five-minute speech, please. Our audience is mostly investors and public officials, so think of a short, clear answer that a busy person can repeat later. My first question is the same for everybody: in your sector, what is the one technology that will be mainstream in ten years, and who will lose if they wait too long? After that, we will open the floor for a twenty-minute question-and-answer session. Let us start with our guest from the legal side.

I ran a container terminal for twelve years, and I want to tell you about the biggest mistake of my career. We were the incumbent. We had a thirty-year concession, good relations with everybody, and a very profitable, labor-intensive business. Every year, my engineers came to me with a plan for automation, and every year I said the same thing: the technology is not ready, let us wait one more year. Then a competitor opened an AI-driven terminal across the bay, and it was not a small improvement. It was a game changer. Ships moved to them in months. When we finally decided to automate, we found a two-year learning curve that nobody had told us about. My advice is simple. You do not need to be the first. But do not be the last.
Ships had a two-day wait at the old terminal.
The old business was labor-intensive and slow.
It was a ten-year contract for an AI-driven terminal.
The incumbent waited too long, and the technology became mainstream without it.
This is a long-term investment, not a quick fix.
Every new system has a learning curve, so we need time to scale up.
You do not need to be the first, but do not be the last.
Long-term contracts need a short, flexible technology clause.
